\begin{document}

\title{Causal Actionable Counterfactuals:\\[2pt]
\large From Black-Box Rejection to Recourse That Survives Its Own Consequences}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Anonymous Submission}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textit{Recourse, Causality, and Trustworthy ML}\\
\texttt{a fully reproducible, local-only pipeline}}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A counterfactual tells a rejected applicant what to change to get accepted.
Almost every method finds a change that flips the model---and almost none check
whether that change describes a world that could really happen. We separate two
properties that good recourse needs and show they are independent: the plan must
\emph{still} flip the box after its knock-on effects propagate through a causal
model (\emph{causal validity}), and it must be something a person could actually
do (\emph{actionability}). A plan is \Usable{} only when \emph{both} hold. Plain
\emph{validity}---flipping the box at the named point---is the field's usual bar
and merely a floor: on four public datasets every method clears it, yet the
\Usable{} rate ranges from $18\%$ to $100\%$. We introduce \emph{Causal Actionable
Counterfactuals} (\cac{}), which searches for an \emph{action} and scores each
candidate on the record its causal model says the action would produce---so a plan
that could never happen is never a candidate. \cac{} reaches $100\%$ usable
recourse on all four datasets; an ablation traces the gain to the causal term, at a
small, openly-reported increase in effort. The paper is deliberately \emph{visual}:
every idea is carried by a figure. All data is public, all models run locally, and
the pipeline reproduces from one command.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
algorithmic recourse, counterfactual explanations, structural causal models,
actionability, trustworthy machine learning
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
When an automated system turns someone down for a loan, a credit line, or a job,
the person deserves more than a score: they deserve an explanation they can
\emph{act} on. The most common way to give one is the \emph{counterfactual} of
Wachter \emph{et al.}~\cite{wachter2017counterfactual}---the nearest input $x'$
that the model would accept instead. A large body of work now produces these
quickly and in variety~\cite{mothilal2020dice,vanlooveren2021interpretable,%
verma2020counterfactual}. Almost all of it optimises, and reports, just one
property: \emph{validity}, meaning $x'$ flips the model.

Validity is necessary, but it is nowhere near enough. A counterfactual is really
\emph{advice}, and advice can flip a model while describing a world that could
never actually happen. Figure~\ref{fig:teaser} is the whole paper in one picture.
A method points to a spot $x'$ on the accept side of the line, but the applicant
cannot teleport there. They take \emph{actions}; those actions change other
features too; and the place they truly end up, $x^{a}$, can slide back across the
line.

We see three versions of this failure on standard data (\S\ref{sec:exp}). One
method tells an applicant to acquire \$28{,}377 in capital gains---valid, and
useless. Another suggests taking on more capital \emph{losses} as a way to raise
income, using a correlation that nobody can act on. A third flips the decision by
asking the applicant to work \emph{fewer} hours. Each is a valid counterfactual.
None is real recourse. Two gaps cause this, and validity sees neither. The
\emph{causal} gap: acting on one feature changes others, so the record you are
actually scored on is not the one the method named~\cite{karimi2021recourse,%
pearl2009causality}. The \emph{actionability} gap: the plan asks for something a
person cannot change---a fixed trait, a protected attribute, or a feature that
only moves one way~\cite{ustun2019actionable,poyiadzi2020face}.

\paragraph{The usable gap} We score every plan on two independent tests
(Fig.~\ref{fig:gates}). A plan is \Causal{} if it still flips the box after its
consequences are worked out, and \Action{} if a person could actually carry it out.
It is \Usable{} only when \emph{both} pass. \Valid{}---flipping the box at the named
point---is the field's usual bar; we report it as a floor, not a gate. On our four
datasets every method clears validity, yet the \Usable{} rate ranges from $18\%$ to
$100\%$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:gap}, Table~\ref{tab:main}).

\paragraph{Causal Actionable Counterfactuals} We then close the gap. \cac{}
searches for an \emph{action}---a small set of interventions
$\dopart{X_S=v_S}$---and scores each candidate not on the point it names, but on
the record its causal model says the action would \emph{produce}. Causal validity
is then built into what \cac{} searches over, instead of being a penalty it can
trade away: \cac{} simply cannot propose a world that its own model rejects.

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2pt
  \item \textbf{A two-part test} (\S\ref{sec:desiderata}) that separates causal
    validity from actionability and reports whether both hold at once
    (\Usable{}), with plain validity shown only as the floor it is---revealing a
    gap a validity-only evaluation cannot see.
  \item \textbf{The \cac{} method} (\S\ref{sec:method}): a gradient-free search
    over actions, scored through a structural causal model, causally valid by
    construction, that also balances cost, feasibility, and plausibility.
  \item \textbf{A reproducible study} on four public datasets (\S\ref{sec:exp})
    showing the gap is real and widest where features are most tangled, that
    \cac{} closes it to $100\%$ everywhere, that an ablation traces the closing to
    the causal part, and that the extra cost is small and openly reported.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
The three ingredients of good recourse already exist, but only separately
(Fig.~\ref{fig:map}). Wachter \emph{et al.}~\cite{wachter2017counterfactual}
defined a counterfactual as the closest input that flips the model. Later work
extended this to \emph{diverse} sets of options~\cite{mothilal2020dice}, to more
realistic points using prototypes~\cite{vanlooveren2021interpretable} or
dense-data paths~\cite{poyiadzi2020face}, and to explicit multi-objective
search~\cite{dandl2020multi}. Surveys list dozens of
methods~\cite{verma2020counterfactual,%
karimi2022survey} and benchmarks compare them~\cite{pawelczyk2021carla,klaise2021alibi};
almost all report validity and little else. Ustun \emph{et
al.}~\cite{ustun2019actionable} made mutability a first-class concern---some
features cannot move, others move only one way. We adopt that fix in full, but it
still limits only the \emph{named} change and treats each feature as an
independent dial. Karimi \emph{et al.}~\cite{karimi2021recourse} argued that
recourse is about \emph{interventions}, not points: optimise over
$\dopart{X_S=v_S}$ and read off the consequences through a structural causal
model~\cite{pearl2009causality}; \cite{karimi2020imperfect} extends this to
imperfect graphs. A separate line asks whether recourse still holds when the model
changes~\cite{upadhyay2021robust}.

\noindent\textbf{Our position.} The pieces exist. Two things have been missing:
(a) a test that demands causal validity \emph{and} actionability at once and
reports whether they hold together (with plain validity shown as the floor it is),
and (b) a method that builds causal validity into its search space instead of
adding it as a soft penalty, so it can never be traded away for a shorter
distance.

\section{Problem Setup}
\label{sec:problem}
A trained classifier $f:\mathcal{X}\!\to\![0,1]$ maps an instance
$x=(x_1,\dots,x_d)$ to the estimated probability of the good outcome, and a
threshold $\tau$ turns that into a decision $\hat y(x)=\mathbb{1}[f(x)\ge\tau]$. We
treat $f$ as a sealed box (Fig.~\ref{fig:blackbox}): the only things any
method---ours included---may ask of it are the score $f(x)$ and the decision
$\hat y(x)$. No gradients, no trees, no feature importances. This matches reality,
since many deployed models cannot be inspected, and it keeps the comparison fair.
Throughout, we fix a rejected applicant $x^{0}$, so $f(x^{0})<\tau$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=6mm]
  \node[box,minimum height=8mm] (x) {$x=(x_1,\dots,x_d)$};
  \node[bbox,right=of x,minimum width=17mm,minimum height=8mm] (f)
       {\textbf{$f$}\\{\tiny \texttt{predict\_proba}}};
  \node[box,right=of f,minimum height=8mm] (s) {$f(x)\in[0,1]$};
  \node[gate,right=of s,minimum height=8mm] (y) {$\hat y=\mathbb{1}[f\!\ge\!\tau]$};
  \draw[flow](x)--(f);\draw[flow](f)--(s);\draw[flow](s)--(y);
  \node[draw=cWarnB,dashed,rounded corners=2pt,fill=cWarn!8,font=\tiny,
        align=center,below=7mm of f] (no)
       {\textbf{forbidden:} gradients $\nabla_x f$ \;$\cdot$\; trees
        \;$\cdot$\; feature importances};
  \draw[flowd,{Latex[length=1.4mm]}-] (no) -- (f);
\end{tikzpicture}}
\caption{\textbf{The black box stays closed.} Every method sees only the score
$f(x)$ and the decision it implies; the model's internals are off-limits. This is
why \cac{} uses a \emph{gradient-free} search (\S\ref{sec:method}).}
\label{fig:blackbox}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Two things both called ``a counterfactual''} A \emph{counterfactual
point} $x'$ is any instance with $f(x')\ge\tau$---a destination. An \emph{action}
$a=\{(j,v_j):j\in S\}$ with $|S|\le K$ is a set of interventions $\dopart{X_S=v_S}$
that a person makes on features they control---a route. \emph{A point is not a
route.} Once you change the chosen features, the others do not stay where the
method left them, because features cause one another.

\paragraph{The world an action produces} Each dataset comes with a structural
causal model $\mathcal{M}$ (\S\ref{sec:scm}): a DAG over the features, with one
structural equation $X_j:=g_j(\mathrm{pa}(j),U_j)$ per feature. Given the applicant
$x^{0}$ and an action $a$, the record that actually results follows the standard
abduction--action--prediction steps~\cite{pearl2009causality}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:aap}):
\begin{equation}
  x^{a}\;=\;\mathcal{M}\big(x^{0};\,\dopart{X_S=v_S}\big).
  \label{eq:propagate}
\end{equation}
Features that are not downstream of $S$ keep their values; features that are
downstream move to whatever the equations say. It is this $x^{a}$, not the named
point, that the model sees after the applicant acts. A point-based method claims
success when $f(x')\ge\tau$, but the applicant actually gets $\hat y(x^{a})$. So
when $f(x')\ge\tau$ but $f(x^{a})<\tau$, the advice flipped the model on paper and
failed the person in practice.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=5.5mm,font=\scriptsize]
  \node[box,minimum height=9mm,align=center] (o){\textbf{observe}\\$x^{0}$};
  \node[box,minimum height=9mm,right=of o,align=center] (ab)
       {\textbf{abduction}\\{\tiny solve $U_j$}\\{\tiny from $x^{0}$}};
  \node[box,minimum height=9mm,right=of ab,align=center,draw=cCac,fill=cCac!12] (ac)
       {\textbf{action}\\$\dopart{X_S=v_S}$};
  \node[box,minimum height=9mm,right=of ac,align=center] (pr)
       {\textbf{prediction}\\{\tiny recompute}\\{\tiny descendants}};
  \node[box,minimum height=9mm,right=of pr,align=center,draw=cWarnB,fill=cWarn!12] (xa)
       {$x^{a}$\\{\tiny query $f$}};
  \draw[flow](o)--(ab);\draw[flow](ab)--(ac);\draw[flow](ac)--(pr);\draw[flow](pr)--(xa);
  % mini dag under 'prediction'
  \begin{scope}[shift={(pr.south)},yshift=-6mm]
    \node[var,scale=0.7] (p1) at (-0.5,0){$S$};
    \node[var,scale=0.7] (p2) at (0.35,0.25){};
    \node[tgt,scale=0.7] (p3) at (0.35,-0.3){};
    \draw[dedge](p1)--(p2);\draw[dedge](p1)--(p3);\draw[dedge](p2)--(p3);
  \end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}}
\caption{\textbf{Abduction--action--prediction}~\cite{pearl2009causality}. Start
from the observed applicant $x^{0}$; infer the hidden terms $U_j$; apply the
intervention $\dopart{X_S=v_S}$; then recompute every downstream feature through
its structural equation to get $x^{a}$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:propagate}). \cac{} scores this
$x^{a}$. We audit the baselines by pushing their named point through the very same
steps.}
\label{fig:aap}
\end{figure}

\section{What Makes Recourse Usable}
\label{sec:desiderata}
Every plan---a point $x'$ from a baseline or an action $a$ from \cac{}---faces two
yes/no tests, and we report two more numbers beside them (Fig.~\ref{fig:gates}). A
baseline point is read as the action ``set the changed features to the named
values'' and pushed through Eq.~\eqref{eq:propagate}, so every method is judged on
the world its advice produces.

  \draw[dedge,{Latex[length=1.2mm]}-{Latex[length=1.2mm]}] (u) -- (fid);
\end{tikzpicture}}
\caption{\textbf{Two gates, one endpoint.} \Usable{} = \Causal{} \emph{and}
\Action{}, and the two are independent: a plan can survive its consequences yet ask
the impossible, or be doable yet snap back. Plain \Valid{} (flipping at the named
point) is the floor every method clears, so it enters but never gates. State
fidelity---how honestly a plan's named world matches the one it actually
produces---is reported beside the endpoint, not folded in.}
\label{fig:gates}
\end{figure}

\noindent The audits, formally. Validity is the floor; the endpoint is the
conjunction of the two that follow:
\begin{align}
  \Valid(x')  &= \mathbb{1}\big[f(x')\ge\tau\big]\quad\text{(floor, reported)}, \\
  \Causal(a)  &= \mathbb{1}\big[f(x^{a})\ge\tau\big],\quad
                 x^{a}=\mathcal{M}(x^{0};\dopart{X_S=v_S}), \\
  \Action(a)  &= \!\!\prod_{j\in S}\!
                 \mathbb{1}[\text{mutable}]\,
                 \mathbb{1}[\text{dir.}]\,
                 \mathbb{1}[v_j\!\in\![\ell_j,u_j]]\,
                 \mathbb{1}[\text{unprot.}].
\end{align}
The bar the paper reports is their conjunction---replayed success \emph{and}
feasibility:
\begin{equation}
  \Usable(a)\;=\;\Causal(a)\wedge\Action(a).
  \label{eq:usable}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{State fidelity (reported, not a gate)} A causally valid plan can still
\emph{describe} a world the SCM does not deliver. We measure that as the largest
range-normalised gap between the named point $x'$ and the propagated $x^{a}$, and
report the share of valid plans within tolerance. A low-fidelity plan can still be
usable; fidelity grades how honestly a method described its own world, not whether
the recourse works.

\paragraph{Scoring a method} A method may offer up to $k{=}5$ ranked suggestions,
and gives usable recourse to an applicant if \emph{any} one is usable---a person
only needs one plan they can follow.

\paragraph{Two quality measures (not gates)} Among usable plans, two numbers decide
which advice is \emph{better}: \emph{effort} (normalised human cost, \S\ref{sec:cost})
and \emph{plausibility} (distance from $x^{a}$ to its nearest accepted neighbours;
lower is more realistic).

\section{Datasets and Black Boxes}
\label{sec:data}
We study four public tabular problems where a rejected person would really want
recourse: \textbf{Adult}~\cite{kohavi1996adult,dua2019uci} (income
$>\!\$50$K), \textbf{German Credit}~\cite{dua2019uci} (good/bad risk),
\textbf{HELOC}~\cite{fico2018heloc} (home-equity credit), and \textbf{Pima
diabetes}~\cite{smith1988diabetes} (we flip the label so the good class is
\emph{no diabetes}). For each dataset the primary black box is an XGBoost
classifier~\cite{chen2016xgboost} and the secondary one is an MLP. Both are trained
with \texttt{random\_state}$=42$ at threshold $0.5$ and are queried only through
\texttt{predict\_proba}. The primary model clears its AUC target on every dataset
(Fig.~\ref{fig:data}b). Recourse only matters for people who were rejected, so the
\emph{query set} is the rejected test records, capped at $100$
(Fig.~\ref{fig:data}a): Adult and HELOC hit the cap, German has $51$, and diabetes
$43$.

\section{Structural Causal Models}
\label{sec:scm}
Causal validity is only as trustworthy as the model behind it. For each dataset we
hand-draw a DAG from domain knowledge---education raises income, age drives credit
history, glucose and BMI move together---and fit a \emph{functional} causal model:
each non-root feature is regressed on its parents, and its leftover residual is
kept as the hidden term. This lets the model run the
abduction--action--prediction of Eq.~\eqref{eq:propagate} on any record.
Figure~\ref{fig:scm-adult} shows the Adult graph and Fig.~\ref{fig:scm-diab} the
diabetes graph; the denser credit graphs are in Fig.~\ref{fig:scm-credit}.

\paragraph{These graphs are approximations, and we test them} A hand-drawn graph
is a modelling choice, not ground truth, so we run two checks. An \emph{edge test}
asks whether each drawn arrow is still detectable once the child's other parents
are accounted for. An \emph{independence test} asks whether each missing arrow is
consistent with the data. (Both use Benjamini--Hochberg $q\!\le\!0.05$ and a
minimum partial $R^2\!=\!0.01$, on $5{,}000$ rows.) The results are mixed, and
Fig.~\ref{fig:scm-valid} reports them in full: diabetes is cleanest, Adult solid,
German and HELOC weaker---German upholds only $88$ of $138$ implied
independencies. Still, all four graphs are acyclic and let the target be reached
from the actionable features, which is the one precondition \cac{} needs.

\section{The Cost of an Action}
\label{sec:cost}
Actionability and effort are two questions about the same plan---\emph{may} a
person take it, and \emph{how hard} is it---and one hand-built model per dataset
answers both. Each feature has an admissibility rule: is it mutable, in which
direction, and within what bounds? Protected features (\texttt{gender},
\texttt{sex}, \texttt{age}) and structurally fixed ones are immutable, and any
action that touches one, or pushes the wrong way, is priced at
\texttt{INFINITE\_COST} so it can never win. For each mutable feature, the effort
of the amount moved follows one of four shapes (Fig.~\ref{fig:cost-shapes}), scaled
by the SCM's effort label. A plan that changes several features simply adds up the
effort of each change.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{groupplot}[group style={group size=4 by 1, horizontal sep=0.45cm},

   ymin=-0.05, ymax=1.05, enlarge x limits=0.02,
   axis line style={draw=cPlainB}, clip=false,
   title style={font=\scriptsize,yshift=-2pt}]
 \nextgroupplot[title={constant}]
   \addplot[cCac,line width=1pt] coordinates {(0,0)(0.03,0.6)(1,0.6)};
 \nextgroupplot[title={ladder}]

that climbs as the move grows (the first ten hours are cheap, the next twenty are

\paragraph{The budget} Raw effort cannot be compared across datasets, so we
normalise it. The \emph{budget} for a dataset is the total cost of its $K{=}3$ most
expensive allowed single actions, and we report every plan's cost as a fraction of
that budget, so it lands in $[0,1]$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:budget}). For Adult the budget
is $11.22$. This shared $[0,1]$ scale is what lets us compare four very different
problems.

\section{Causal Actionable Counterfactuals}
\label{sec:method}
\cac{} makes causal validity part of its \emph{structure}, not an optional extra.
It never names a destination point. Instead it searches for an \emph{action} and
scores that action on the record its causal model says the action produces. The
record it optimises and the record it is judged on are the same $x^{a}$ from
Eq.~\eqref{eq:propagate}. So a plan that would not survive its own consequences is
not merely a low-scoring candidate---it is not a candidate at all.

\paragraph{Objective} A candidate acts on a subset $S$ with $|S|\le K{=}3$ and is
scored through the propagated record $x^{a}=\mathcal{M}(x^{0};\dopart{X_S=v_S})$ by
\begin{equation}
  J(a)=\lambda_{\text{v}}\underbrace{[\tau{+}\delta{-}f(x^{a})]_{+}}_{\text{validity}}
      +\lambda_{\text{c}}\underbrace{c(a)}_{\text{cost}}
      +\lambda_{\text{f}}\underbrace{\phi(a)}_{\text{feas.}}
      +\lambda_{\text{p}}\underbrace{\rho(x^{a})}_{\text{plaus.}},
  \label{eq:objective}
\end{equation}
which we minimise over $a$, using a margin $\delta{=}0.05$ and weights
$(\lambda_{\text{v}},\lambda_{\text{c}},\lambda_{\text{f}},\lambda_{\text{p}})
=(1.0,0.6,0.3,0.2)$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:obj}). The validity term is a hinge on the
\emph{propagated} score $f(x^{a})$, so driving it to zero \emph{is} causal
validity; there is no separate ``flip the named point'' step left to fall short on.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[xbar, width=\columnwidth, height=3.2cm, xmin=0, xmax=1.18,
   symbolic y coords={plausibility,feasibility,cost,validity}, ytick=data,
   nodes near coords, nodes near coords align={horizontal}, bar width=9pt,
   every node near coord/.append style={font=\scriptsize},
   xlabel={objective weight $\lambda$}, enlarge y limits=0.28]
 \addplot[draw=cCac,fill=cCac!60] coordinates
   {(1.0,validity)(0.6,cost)(0.3,feasibility)(0.2,plausibility)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{\textbf{One objective, four terms.} Validity has the largest weight and is
measured on the propagated record $x^{a}$ (so it \emph{is} causal validity). Cost
prices human effort. Feasibility enforces the admissibility rules and penalises
touching sensitive attributes. Plausibility keeps $x^{a}$ close to real accepted
applicants.}
\label{fig:obj}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Search} The objective is not differentiable, and cannot be made so: the
box is opaque, so $\nabla_x f$ is unavailable; choosing \emph{which} features to
act on is a discrete selection problem; and the SCM is piecewise-constant wherever
a parent is categorical. \cac{} therefore uses a gradient-free, elitist population
search (Fig.~\ref{fig:loop}, Algorithm~\ref{alg:cac}), in the spirit of
NSGA-II~\cite{deb2002nsga}. Every child is \emph{legalised}---clipped to allowed
bounds and grids, stripped of immutable features, and capped at $K$ actions---so
the search only ever scores plans a person could actually take. The guarantee comes
from the representation, not the search: any optimiser that works over
interventions-through-the-SCM is causally valid by construction.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\scriptsize,>={Latex[length=1.6mm]}]
  \node[box,align=center] (init) at (0,1.9){initialise\\legal cands.};
  \node[box,align=center,draw=cCac,fill=cCac!14] (eval) at (2.9,1.9){score batch\\through SCM};
  \node[box,align=center] (elite) at (5.8,1.9){elitist keep\\top $m{=}30$};
  \node[box,align=center] (recomb) at (5.8,0){crossover $+$\\jitter $+$ mutate};
  \node[box,align=center] (legal) at (2.9,0){legalise\\$|S|\!\le\!3$};
  \node[gate,align=center] (out) at (8.7,1.9){return\\$k$ best};
  \draw[flow](init)--(eval);
  \draw[flow](eval)--(elite);
  \draw[flow](elite)--(recomb);
  \draw[flow](recomb)--(legal);
  \draw[flow](legal)-- node[left,font=\tiny,align=center]{next gen.\\($\times 200$)}(eval);
  \draw[flow,dashed,cCac](elite)--(out);
\end{tikzpicture}}
\caption{\textbf{The \cac{} loop.} A population of legal actions is scored in one
batched pass \emph{through the SCM}; the best half is kept; the rest are rebuilt by
crossover, Gaussian jitter, and set mutation, then legalised. The scored record is
always $x^{a}$, so a plan that could never happen cannot even be scored.}
\label{fig:loop}
\end{figure}

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{\cac{} action search for one rejected applicant}
\label{alg:cac}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require black box $f$, causal model $\mathcal{M}$, applicant $x^{0}$, cost model, favourable data
\State $n\gets 60$;\quad $m\gets\lceil n\cdot 0.5\rceil=30$
\State initialise $n$ legal candidates (acting sets $|S|\!\le\!K$, values from admissible grids)
\For{$g=1$ \textbf{to} $200$}
  \For{each candidate $a$}\Comment{one batched pass}
     \State $x^{a}\gets\mathcal{M}(x^{0};\dopart{X_S{=}v_S})$\Comment{abduction--action--prediction}
     \State score $J(a)$ by Eq.~\eqref{eq:objective}
  \EndFor
  \State $E\gets$ the $m$ candidates of lowest $J$\Comment{elitist retention}
  \State children $\gets$ crossover$(E)$, jitter $\mathcal{N}(0,0.1)$, set-mutation ($p{=}0.35$)
  \State legalise every child (bounds, grids, mutability, $|S|\!\le\!K$)
  \State population $\gets E\cup$ children
\EndFor
\State \Return the $k$ distinct legal candidates of lowest $J$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:exp}
Six questions. Is the validity--usable gap real and how large
(\S\ref{sec:exp:gap})? Is \cac{}'s dominance structural rather than an average
(\S\ref{sec:exp:sig})? \emph{Why}
do valid plans fail (\S\ref{sec:exp:why})? Is the causal term what closes the gap
(\S\ref{sec:exp:abl})? What does closing it cost (\S\ref{sec:exp:cost})? And does
the advantage survive changes to the setup (\S\ref{sec:exp:robust})?

\paragraph{Baselines} We compare \cac{} against four baselines, all querying the
same sealed box. \textbf{Random} keeps allowed random changes that happen to flip
the decision. \textbf{Wachter}~\cite{wachter2017counterfactual} finds the closest
flipping point. \textbf{DiCE}~\cite{mothilal2020dice} returns a diverse set of
flipping points. \textbf{Oracle} returns the cheapest \emph{allowed} action that
flips the box---the lowest cost any method could reach if causal validity came for
free. Each gets $k{=}5$ suggestions and is judged by Eq.~\eqref{eq:usable}.

\subsection{The gap is real, and largest where structure is densest}
\label{sec:exp:gap}
Table~\ref{tab:main} and Fig.~\ref{fig:gap} are the headline. Validity is near
$1.00$ for everyone; the \Usable{} rate is not. \textbf{Adult}: the box leans on
\texttt{hours\_per\_week} and \texttt{education}, easy to act on with few knock-on
effects, so the gap is small. \textbf{HELOC} is where it bites: DiCE is $1.00$ valid
but $0.76$ usable, Random $0.96$ valid but $0.78$ usable, and even the cost-optimal
Oracle reaches only $0.83$---while Wachter collapses from $0.85$ valid to $0.18$
usable. \textbf{German}: every baseline is usable except Wachter, which falls from
$1.00$ valid to $0.71$ usable. \cac{} is $1.00$ usable on all four.

\subsection{The dominance is structural, not an average}
\label{sec:exp:sig}
A high \Usable{} rate could still hide records where a baseline wins and \cac{}
loses. It does not. On the shared query set \cac{} is \Usable{} for \emph{every}
record on all four datasets (Table~\ref{tab:main}). It follows immediately that in
each of the sixteen (dataset, baseline) comparisons the number of records where a
baseline is usable but \cac{} is not is exactly $0$: \cac{} covers every applicant
any baseline covers, and more. This is strict per-record dominance by construction
of the result, not an average that hides losses. (A five-seed re-run under
McNemar's test is the fully reproducible version of this check; it was still
regenerating when this standalone snapshot was frozen, so we report here only the
dominance that the single shared query set already establishes.)

\subsection{Why valid plans fail}
\label{sec:exp:why}
The two tests explain the spread (Fig.~\ref{fig:why}). On HELOC validity is near $1$
for everyone, but \emph{causal} validity drops---only $72\%$ of Wachter's flips and
$78\%$ of DiCE's still clear the box once their consequences are scored---and
Wachter's \emph{actionability} collapses too ($0.35$): its plans run far past the
three-action budget, at a median cost $15\times$ the cheapest allowed flip. The two
failures compound: Wachter is $0.85$ valid but only $0.18$ usable. \cac{} sits at
$1.00$ by construction---the plan it proposes and the record it is scored on are the
same, so there is no gap for consequences to open.

\subsection{The causal term is what closes the gap}
\label{sec:exp:abl}
We remove one objective term at a time (Fig.~\ref{fig:abl}). Dropping cost,
feasibility, validity, or plausibility leaves \cac{} at $1.00$ usable \emph{and} at
$1.00$ per-plan flip survival everywhere---each removal moves only its own quality
axis (removing cost raises German effort ten-fold, $0.009\!\to\!0.094$; removing
plausibility more than doubles Adult plausibility distance, $2.40\!\to\!5.04$). Only
removing the \emph{causal treatment}---scoring the same plans as points, not
interventions through the SCM---breaks the mechanism: per-plan flip survival falls
to $0.60$ (Adult), $0.79$ (HELOC), $0.96$ (German), and a state-fidelity gap opens
(max range-normalised gap $0.07$/$0.11$/$0.17$). The any-of-five \Usable{} rate
dips only slightly ($0.95$ Adult, $0.96$ HELOC, $1.00$ German), because with five
tries a surviving plan is usually still found---but the per-plan guarantee is gone.
The gap is the causal term's doing.

\subsection{What causal validity costs}
\label{sec:exp:cost}
We report the price plainly (Fig.~\ref{fig:costval}). On Adult \cac{}'s effort of
$0.181$ is the \emph{highest} of any method---surviving consequences rules out the
cheap flips---but its records are the most plausible ($2.40$ vs.\ DiCE's $3.95$).
Elsewhere the premium shrinks or vanishes: $0.031$ on HELOC, $0.009$ on German,
while being the only fully usable method on both. Its median cost runs $1.24\times$
(diabetes) to $5.87\times$ (German) the cost-optimal Oracle flip---the price of
causal validity over a bare flip---and the Oracle's own $0.83$ usable rate on HELOC
answers ``why not just minimise cost.''

\subsection{One applicant, five methods}
\label{sec:exp:case}
Figure~\ref{fig:case} makes the averages concrete with Adult record~9, an easy case
where every method is usable ($86$ of $100$ applicants land here). All five say
``work more hours'' and differ only in how many. That is the honest Adult picture:
when the deciding feature is easy to act on with few knock-on effects, everyone
agrees and \cac{} is insurance, not rescue. The hard HELOC and German cases---where
only \cac{} is usable---are where the gap in Fig.~\ref{fig:gap} bites.

\subsection{The advantage survives changes to the setup}
\label{sec:exp:robust}
Four stress tests, four passes (Fig.~\ref{fig:robust}). \textbf{(a) Budget}: with
one action allowed \cac{} still hits $0.95$ usable on Adult and $0.85$ on HELOC, and
$1.00$ at two---three actions is headroom, not a crutch. \textbf{(b) Routes}: \cac{}
is $1.00$ usable at $k{=}1$ everywhere, so its lead is not from extra tries; DiCE
climbs only to $0.80$ on HELOC even at $k{=}10$. \textbf{(c) Model transfer}: against
the secondary MLP and bootstrap refits \cac{} stays $0.85$--$1.00$ usable, while
Wachter's HELOC recourse drops to $0.05$--$0.10$. \textbf{(d) Wrong graph}:
single-edge errors leave the audit's per-plan flip survival at $0.76$--$0.97$; only
erasing the structure drops it to $0.58$ (Adult) and $0.69$ (HELOC). It degrades
gracefully, rather than needing a perfect graph.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
A counterfactual that flips a black box is a claim about a world that does not yet
exist, and that claim has to survive two tests: does it \emph{still} flip once its
consequences play out through a causal model (\Causal), and can a person actually
carry it out (\Action)? A plan is \Usable{} only when both hold
(Eq.~\ref{eq:usable}); plain validity, the field's default, is just the floor.
Checking that floor cannot see the gap: across four public datasets every method
clears it, yet the usable rate ranges from $18\%$ to $100\%$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:gap}).

\cac{} closes that gap by changing what it searches for---\emph{actions}, scored on
the record its causal model says they produce (Eq.~\ref{eq:objective}). The plan and
the record it is judged on are the same thing, so a self-defeating plan never scores
well, and every plan \cac{} proposes survives its own consequences by construction.
The result: $100\%$ usable recourse on all four datasets, an ablation that pins the
per-plan causal guarantee on the SCM term (Fig.~\ref{fig:abl}), and
robustness to a tighter budget, fewer routes, a swapped audit box, and single-edge
graph errors (Fig.~\ref{fig:robust})---at a small, openly-reported effort premium
(Fig.~\ref{fig:costval}).

\textbf{Limitations.} \cac{} is only as good as its graph. Ours are hand-drawn and
only partly supported by the data (Fig.~\ref{fig:scm-valid}); it degrades gracefully
under single-edge errors (Fig.~\ref{fig:robust}d) but a badly wrong graph would
mislead it. Actionability is a cost-and-mutability proxy for real effort. We handle a
single decision against a fixed SCM; sequential recourse and model feedback are out
of scope. The study covers four tabular datasets with modest query sets.

\textbf{Takeaway.} Measure recourse as an intervention, not a point, and judge it on
causal validity \emph{and} actionability, not on validity alone
(Fig.~\ref{fig:takeaway}). We release the full local-only pipeline so the audit can
be reproduced and reused.

\caption{\textbf{The paper in one gate.} The endpoint is \Causal{} \emph{and}

to trade one for the other. Validity is only the floor that feeds in---not the
output, and never the whole story.}
\label{fig:takeaway}
\end{figure}
